learningObjectives.title: The role of government and limitations of markets

questions.q: In the UK, the rate of inflation is officially measured using the:
questions.explain: Inflation is measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), which tracks the change in the average price of a basket of goods and services.

questions.q: The UK government's target rate of inflation, which the Bank of England aims to achieve, is:
questions.explain: The Bank of England is set a symmetrical CPI inflation target of 2% by the government.

questions.q: In the UK, decisions on interest rates are made by the:
options: Monetary Policy Committee of the Bank of England
questions.explain: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets the base interest rate to help meet the inflation target.

questions.q: Fiscal policy is the use of:
options: Interest rates and the money supply
questions.explain: Fiscal policy involves changing levels of government spending and taxation to influence the economy.

questions.q: Economic growth is best measured by an increase in:
questions.explain: Economic growth is measured by the increase in real GDP, the total value of output adjusted for inflation.

questions.q: A public good, such as national defence, is defined as being:
options: Only ever provided by private firms
questions.explain: Public goods are non-excludable (people cannot be prevented from using them) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce availability to others).

questions.q: Unemployment caused by a fall in demand during a recession is known as:
questions.explain: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment occurs when a lack of aggregate demand in a downturn reduces the need for workers.

questions.q: A sustained fall in the general price level in an economy is called:
questions.explain: Deflation is a sustained fall in the average price level, the opposite of inflation.

questions.q: The main aim of supply-side policies is to:
options: Increase the productive capacity of the economy
Fix the value of the exchange rate
questions.explain: Supply-side policies, such as training and deregulation, aim to increase the economy's productive potential and efficiency.

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is most likely to be caused by:
options: A reduction in the money supply
questions.explain: Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than supply, pulling prices upwards.

questions.q: A merit good, such as education, tends to be under-consumed in a free market because:
options: Consumers do not fully value its private and social benefits
It is over-priced by the government
questions.explain: Merit goods are under-consumed because individuals undervalue the long-term benefits to themselves and to society.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a negative externality?
options: Air pollution from a factory harming local residents
A consumer buying a loaf of bread
questions.explain: A negative externality is a cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction, such as pollution affecting residents.

questions.q: An increase in interest rates by the Bank of England is most likely to:
questions.explain: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing spending and easing inflation.

questions.q: A regressive tax is one where:
options: The proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises
Higher earners pay a higher proportion of their income
Everyone pays exactly the same amount
Only businesses are required to pay
questions.explain: With a regressive tax, lower-income earners pay a larger share of their income than higher-income earners.

questions.q: Cigarettes are usually classed as a demerit good because they are:
options: Over-consumed and cause harm to the user and others
questions.explain: Demerit goods are over-consumed because people underestimate the private and external costs they create.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes monetary policy from fiscal policy?
options: Monetary policy uses interest rates while fiscal policy uses spending and taxation
Both are controlled by the Chancellor of the Exchequer
Monetary policy changes tax rates and fiscal policy sets interest rates
Both rely only on changing the exchange rate
questions.explain: Monetary policy (Bank of England) works through interest rates and the money supply, while fiscal policy (government) uses spending and taxation.

questions.q: During a recession, a government cuts income tax to boost demand. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Cutting taxation to increase demand and output is expansionary fiscal policy.

questions.q: CPI inflation rises to 6%, well above target. The Bank of England is most likely to respond by:
questions.explain: To bring inflation back towards the 2% target, the Bank of England would raise interest rates to reduce spending.

questions.q: A chemical plant dumps waste into a river, harming a downstream fishing business. To correct this market failure, the government could:
options: Impose a tax or regulation on the polluter
Give the chemical plant a subsidy
Do nothing, as the market will self-correct
Lower interest rates for the fishing business
questions.explain: Taxes and regulation make the polluter bear the external cost, discouraging the harmful activity and correcting the market failure.

questions.q: A government funds free apprenticeship and training schemes to improve workers' skills. This is best described as a:
questions.explain: Improving skills raises productivity and the economy's productive capacity, which is the aim of supply-side policy.
